title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
DNA is fixed for life, but proteins change with diet, disease, drugs and age, and they are what actually does the work in cells. Most drugs act on proteins. That makes the proteome, all the proteins in a sample, an attractive layer for finding biomarkers and drug targets.
Measuring proteins is harder than reading DNA. Plasma contains proteins at concentrations that differ by many orders of magnitude, the same gene can give several protein forms, and most methods measure how much protein there is, not how well it works. Modern platforms (Olink, SomaScan) now measure thousands of proteins in tens of thousands of people, which allows proteome-wide association studies (PWAS), the protein version of a GWAS.
The second half connects proteins back to genetics. A SNP that changes a protein’s level is a pQTL. If it sits next to the protein’s own gene (cis-pQTL), it is a good instrument for protein Mendelian randomization: does genetically higher protein cause disease? The lecture closes the course’s PCSK9 story end to end.
This page covers why and where to measure proteins, the three technology families, what the numbers mean (NPX), QC and batch effects, PWAS, pQTLs (cis vs trans), protein MR and its specific pitfalls, colocalization and the path from association to mechanism.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.1 Why study the proteome?
Contrast from the molecular-layer table (Lecture 1): DNA is fixed, while RNA and proteins are dynamic, affected by diet, disease, drugs, environment and age. Proteins matter because they carry out cellular functions, act as signalling molecules, respond to disease/environment/diet/drugs/age, and are the targets of most drugs (Leqvio and Repatha in Lecture 3).
Worked example: insulin biosynthesis. “One gene” does not always mean “one direct protein”:
INS gene ─transcription─▶ INS mRNA ─translation─▶ preproinsulin
   ─signal peptide removed─▶ proinsulin
   ─folds, forms disulfide bonds, C-peptide cleaved out─▶ insulin + C-peptide
(Insulin is a signalling molecule central to metabolism, obesity and diabetes; compare the glucose/insulin example in Lecture 1.)
Proteins are not 1-to-1 with genes. Processes that multiply protein products:







Process
Example




Alternative splicing
One gene’s transcript spliced into several mRNA/protein variants


Cleavage
Insulin from proinsulin


Post-translational modification (PTM)
Phosphorylation, glycosylation, cleavage


Different cellular localization
Same sequence behaves differently depending on where it ends up


Protein complexes
Proteins assemble into larger units (quaternary structure, Lecture 1)



Net effect: the proteome is more dynamic and complex than the genome.






ImportantProtein amount ≠ protein function



More protein does not automatically mean more function (though in the simplest case it does). The same amount can have different function, e.g. after a GoF or LoF mutation (the PCSK9 examples in Lecture 3): a functionally altered protein can be present at a normal concentration. Most proteomics methods measure amount (abundance), not function.



  Every gene is translated into exactly one protein product
  Splicing, cleavage and modifications create extra variants
  Proteins are copied directly from other proteins in the cell
  The genome changes continuously with diet and age
  Alternative splicing, cleavage, post-translational modifications, localization and complex formation all multiply the number of distinct protein products per gene.

8.5 What a protein measurement means: units and NPX








Kind
Meaning
Units




Absolute concentration
Real physical amount
mg/dL (US), mmol/L (EU), ng/mL or pg/mL for low-abundance proteins


Relative abundance
Relationships between samples are meaningful, the numbers are not physical concentrations
Often normalized, log-transformed, arbitrary units



Platform units

Olink and SomaScan: relative abundance as NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression) on a log₂ scale. One NPX unit = a doubling of signal (same logic as log₂FC in Lecture 7).
Mass spectrometry: peptide intensity, ion counts or peak area; often calibrated by spiking in a labelled peptide of known concentration as an internal standard.


  The first person has 3 times as much
  The first person has 8 times as much
  The first person has 3 mg/dL more
  They differ by 3% in concentration
  NPX is log₂: a difference of 3 NPX means 2³ = 8 times the relative abundance. It says nothing about absolute mg/dL.

section: 8.6 QC, pre-analytical variation and batch effects
text:
8.6 QC, pre-analytical variation and batch effects
Pipeline: individual → blood sample → plasma/serum → assay → [QC, batch-effect handling, sample-prep issues such as freeze/thaw] → protein table (one row per person, one column per protein, e.g. Protein 1 … Protein 3000). Same shape as the GWAS table in Lecture 5, with continuous protein values instead of dosages.
QC at two levels







Sample-level QC
Protein-level QC




Was the sample measured successfully?
Is the protein reliably detected across samples?


Is it an outlier across many proteins (a sample-wide problem)?
Too much missingness for this protein?


Too much missingness for this sample?
Is the assay reproducible?


Did internal technical controls fail?
Is its variation dominated by batch rather than biology?



A very high or low value can be: real biology, contamination, technical failure, assay saturation (signal maxed out) or a processing error. Technical controls (for sample processing, hybridization/amplification, assay performance, normalization) help separate biology from artifact.
Pre-analytical variation (before the lab assay, often overlooked): fasting vs non-fasting, time of day, posture and recent exercise, tube/anticoagulant, time from draw to centrifugation, storage temperature, number of freeze–thaw cycles, hemolysis (red cells rupturing into the plasma), delay before freezing.






WarningSystematic, not random



Sick patients may be handled differently (more time, more controlled) than controls (processed faster, more randomly). Centers may have different protocols, and protocols change over time. If handling correlates with disease status, you get systematic bias.


Batch effects. A batch is any group of samples processed together that may share an artifact: the same plate, reagent lot, lab run, day, instrument or operator.
Detection: boxplots by plate/run (systematic shifts), PCA (do samples cluster by batch rather than biology?), clustering, technical controls, replicate samples across batches, comparing value distributions across plates.








Prevent: design stage
Correct: analysis stage




Randomize samples across plates
Normalize across platforms/batches


Balance cases and controls across plates/batches
Adjust for plate/run as a covariate


Technical replicate samples across plates
Include batch as a covariate in the regression (like genotyping batch in GWAS, Lecture 4)


Common reference samples repeated across plates





Transformations for proteomics data (right-skewed, wide dynamic range, sensitive to extremes):

log transformation compresses the right tail;
z-scores \(z = \dfrac{x - \text{mean}(x)}{\text{SD}(x)}\) (mean 0, SD 1) make effect sizes comparable across proteins on different scales;
plate normalization;
reference-sample normalization: the same sample on every plate, and all values on a plate normalized to it, removing plate-to-plate drift.


  The study cannot use NPX units for relative abundance
  Batch is completely confounded with case status
  Too few proteins are measured on each individual plate
  The protein values will no longer be right-skewed
  Any plate effect is indistinguishable from the case–control difference. Randomizing and balancing cases and controls across plates at the design stage prevents this; no analysis step can fully fix it afterwards.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.7 The proteome-wide association study (PWAS)
Same structure as a GWAS, with a protein instead of a SNP as the predictor:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{protein} + \beta_2 \times \text{age} + \beta_3 \times \text{sex} + \dots\]
If the protein is standardized (z-score), \(\beta\) is the effect of a 1-SD higher protein level:

continuous \(Y\): \(\beta = 0.18\) → 0.18 units higher outcome per SD;
binary \(Y\) (logistic): \(e^{0.18} \approx 1.20\) → 20% higher odds per SD.

Two model directions







Protein as predictor
Protein as outcome




\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{protein} + \text{covariates}\)
\(\text{protein} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{exposure} + \text{covariates}\)


Does this protein predict the phenotype?
Does this exposure predict the protein level?



Multiple testing in PWAS. ~3,000 proteins → about \(3{,}000 \times 0.05 = 150\) false positives at uncorrected \(p < 0.05\). In discovery, control the FDR (usually BH, Lecture 7). Unlike GWAS, there is no single conventional threshold like 5×10⁻⁸: it depends on the number of proteins, their correlation and the strategy.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.8 Association is still not causation
Three explanations for a protein–disease association:
protein ──▶ disease            causal
disease ──▶ protein            reverse causation (disease changes the protein)
protein ◀── confounder ──▶ disease   confounding
A protein can be a good biomarker/predictor without being causal. Troponin marks cardiac injury, but lowering troponin would not treat an MI: it is a readout of injury that already happened. Prediction and causation are different properties; only some proteins have both.

  Troponin cannot be measured in plasma with current assays
  It is released by injury, a consequence of the infarction
  Troponin levels are fixed at conception like DNA
  It is a trans-pQTL, so it has horizontal pleiotropy
  Troponin is a readout of cardiomyocyte damage. Lowering it would not undo the damage: prediction without causation.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.9 pQTLs: connecting genetics and proteomics
For a given SNP, do genotype groups (AA = 0, AG = 1, GG = 2) differ in protein abundance?
\[\text{Protein} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Genotype} + \varepsilon\]
(The SNP → continuous phenotype model of Lecture 4 with protein level as the outcome.) Questions it answers: which variants regulate which circulating proteins? Which genes influence protein levels? Can a protein be linked genetically to disease? Can the variant be an MR instrument?
pQTL (protein quantitative trait locus): a SNP associated with a protein’s abundance.






WarningA SNP can change function without changing abundance



Since assays measure amount, a functionally important variant can be invisible to a pQTL analysis if it does not also change the concentration.


PCSK9 chain: PCSK9 SNP → circulating PCSK9 protein → LDL receptor activity → LDL-C. DNA to clinical biomarker in four steps.










cis-pQTL
trans-pQTL




Location
Close to the gene encoding the protein
Far away: common working definition > 500 kb, or a different chromosome


Plausible mechanisms
Transcription, splicing, protein stability or secretion of that gene’s product
Indirect: transcription factors, receptors, signalling pathways, protein-processing machinery


Interpretation
Relatively direct biological interpretation
More indirect


As MR instrument
Preferred
Higher risk of horizontal pleiotropy





  A cis-pQTL, because it changes protein abundance
  A trans-pQTL, because it is far from the encoding gene
  A cis-pQTL, because any SNP near a gene counts as cis
  Not a pQTL, because pQTLs must be on the same gene
  cis = near the encoding gene; trans = far away (> 500 kb) or on another chromosome. Different chromosome → trans.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.10 Protein Mendelian randomization
Genetic variant → protein abundance → disease risk. With \(\beta_{GP}\) = SNP effect on Protein and \(\beta_{GO}\) = SNP effect on Outcome:
\[\hat\beta_{MR} = \frac{\beta_{GO}}{\beta_{GP}}\]
The Wald ratio of Lecture 6 with protein level as the exposure: the effect on the outcome per genetically predicted unit change in protein.
Why cis-pQTLs are preferred as instruments: closer to the encoding gene, so an easier and more direct biological link, and less risk of horizontal pleiotropy (fewer alternative pathways than a variant acting at a distance). But cis-pQTLs still need all three MR assumptions (relevance, independence, exclusion restriction). Being cis reduces one risk; it does not remove the need for the other checks.

  0.05 log-odds per SD of protein X
  0.20 log-odds per SD of protein X
  5.0 log-odds per SD of protein X
  0.60 log-odds per SD of protein X
  β_MR = β_GO / β_GP = 0.10 / 0.5 = 0.20 per SD, i.e. OR ≈ e^0.2 ≈ 1.22 per SD higher genetically predicted protein X.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.11 Challenges specific to protein MR







Challenge
Why it matters




Horizontal pleiotropy
Violates the exclusion restriction; especially relevant for trans-pQTLs


Assay binding artifacts
A coding variant can change the protein’s structure so the antibody/aptamer binds worse, giving a seemingly lower level with no real change in amount. Fairly unique to protein instruments


Amount ≠ function
A variant can change activity, binding, stability or localization without changing measured abundance


LD can fake causality
SNP A affects the protein, a different SNP B in LD affects disease through another mechanism: protein and disease look linked only through the LD


One pQTL, many proteins
SNP → protein A, B and C at once; the effect may not run through the one protein you study



Colocalization: is it the same signal? Compare the pattern of association across a region for the protein’s pQTL and for the disease GWAS. If one shared causal variant drives both, SNPs in LD should give a matching pattern of association strength for both traits. If the patterns do not line up, the protein and disease associations are probably driven by two distinct (possibly nearby) causal variants. Check this before concluding that a pQTL and a GWAS hit at “the same locus” reflect the same biology.

  The variant may change assay binding, not the amount
  The variant must be a trans-pQTL since it is missense
  The variant cannot affect protein function at all
  The variant proves the protein causes the disease
  Coding variants can alter the epitope the antibody or aptamer binds, producing an apparent drop in abundance: an assay binding artifact.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.12 From association to confirmed mechanism
The lecture’s pipeline:
protein association → pQTL evidence → MR / colocalization
   → candidate causal protein → mechanistic experiments → biological pathway
Follow-up questions once a protein is genetically implicated: Which cell or tissue produces it? Which receptor or pathway does it act through? Does changing its level or activity change cell function? Does it reproduce in an experimental model? Can the pathway be modified by a drug (is it druggable)?
Experimental validation approaches: CRISPR knock-out or knock-in; protein overexpression or targeted inhibition; cultured cells; organoids; animal models; receptor-binding experiments; enzyme activity assays.

The PCSK9 story, end to end (be able to reproduce it from memory)







Step





Genetics
PCSK9 genetic variation


Protein
PCSK9 protein abundance


Mechanism
PCSK9 promotes LDLR degradation → fewer LDL receptors on hepatocytes


Physiology
Reduced LDL clearance → higher LDL-C


Disease
Higher atherosclerotic risk


Drug (mirror image)
PCSK9 inhibition (Repatha/Praluent block the protein; Leqvio silences the mRNA) → more LDLR → lower LDL-C










ImportantClosing statement of the course’s method arc



A protein can be statistically associated, genetically supported (pQTL/MR) and still need experimental validation before you understand the mechanism. This echoes Lecture 1: molecular epidemiology is not biology.

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
Observational studies keep finding that people with high LDL cholesterol get more heart disease, but that alone cannot prove LDL causes it: smokers might have both, or early disease might change LDL. The gold standard answer is a randomized trial. Mendelian randomization (MR) uses a trial that nature already ran: at conception, each person is randomly dealt alleles that raise or lower LDL a little.
If people who inherited LDL-raising alleles also have more heart disease, and those alleles do nothing else relevant, the most plausible explanation is that LDL itself causes heart disease. Genotype cannot be changed by the disease, so reverse causation is ruled out from the start.
The whole method stands or falls on three assumptions about the genetic instrument: it must affect the exposure (relevance), it must not share causes with the outcome (independence), and it must affect the outcome only through the exposure (exclusion restriction). Most of the lecture is about checking those assumptions, especially the last one, which horizontal pleiotropy breaks.
This page covers imputation and proxy SNPs, the Bradford Hill criteria, why genes are good instruments, confounding, the three assumptions with their named threats, vertical vs horizontal pleiotropy, the Wald ratio and IVW estimate, weighted median and MR-Egger, and how to interpret an MR result. This is the lecture that ties the course together.

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.1 Imputation and proxy SNPs
The problem. You want to know whether a specific variant (rsXY) affects a phenotype, but it was not measured in your data. Or: your data has SNPs + SBP, another dataset tested the same region against stroke, but the SNP overlap is poor: your lead SNPs are missing in the other dataset and vice versa. Dead end?
Two tools solve it, both using LD structure:







Tool
How it works




Proxy SNP
A SNP in very strong LD (\(r^2\) close to 1) with the SNP you want. It carries essentially the same signal, so it can stand in for it


Imputation
Uses LD patterns plus a large external reference panel to predict the genotype at a missing SNP as a (linear) combination of the measured SNPs, e.g. \(\text{SNP}_3 = \sum_{i \in \{3,5,6,8,11\}} a_i \cdot \text{SNP}_i\) (illustrative)



Both bridge the gap between studies (or a study and a reference panel) that did not measure exactly the same SNPs.

Criterion
Short meaning




1

2
Consistency

3

One exposure linked to one outcome


4

Exposure comes before outcome (the only strictly necessary one)


5
Biological gradient
Dose–response


6

7

9

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.3 Genetic variants as instruments
Key insight: genetic variants are natural instrumental variables. Genotype is fixed at conception, so it comes first in any causal chain: no reverse causation (adult disease cannot change the genotype you were born with).
Genetic variant (SNP) ──▶ Exposure ──▶ Outcome
To use a SNP to study the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome, three core assumptions must hold: relevance, independence, exclusion restriction (Section 6.5 gives them in full).

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.4 Why we need MR: confounding
Motivating problem. Does LDL-C cause coronary heart disease (CHD)? Observationally, high LDL-C precedes CHD, but how do you rule out:

confounding, e.g. smoking affects both: LDL-C ← SMOKING → CHD
selection bias
measurement error
reverse causation (which came first?)

The classical gold standard is the randomized controlled trial (RCT): intervene on LDL-C and see whether CHD risk changes. RCTs are expensive, slow, and not always ethical or feasible.
The genetic parallel. A naturally occurring SNP that raises or lowers LDL-C is allocated at random at conception, because meiosis randomly allocates alleles to offspring, much as an RCT randomly allocates treatment. Hence Mendelian randomization: SNP → LDL-C → CHD.










RCT
Mendelian randomization




Random allocation
Treatment assigned by researcher
Alleles assigned at meiosis


“Intervention”
Drug lowers LDL-C
Allele lowers LDL-C (lifelong)


Confounding
Balanced by randomization
Balanced, if the independence assumption holds


Reverse causation
Excluded by design
Excluded: genotype fixed at conception




Why is a GWAS association with CHD not enough? It says a SNP is associated with CHD (or LDL-C), not which pathway or which gene. The SNP could act through LDL-C, or through inflammation or blood pressure (SBP). MR is designed to resolve this.

section: 6.5 Instruments and the three MR assumptions
text:
6.5 Instruments and the three MR assumptions
Selecting instruments. Choose SNPs strongly associated with the exposure (e.g. LDL-C), typically \(P < 5 \times 10^{-8}\) in the exposure GWAS, and independent of each other (low LD, e.g. \(r^2 < 0.01\), via LD clumping, Lecture 5). At this stage you do not look at the SNP → outcome relationship at all; that comes in later.






ImportantThe three MR assumptions (the most important definitional block in the course)












#
Assumption
Meaning
Named threats




1
Relevance
The variant has a robust, strong association with the exposure. Usually checked by genome-wide significance in the exposure GWAS
Weak instruments bias and destabilize the estimate


2
Independence
The variant is not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship
Population stratification, assortative mating (non-random mate choice related to the trait), selection effects (participation depends on genotype and outcome)


3
Exclusion restriction
The variant affects the outcome only through the exposure
Horizontal pleiotropy: another pathway. Ask: “does this SNP affect the outcome through another pathway entirely?”





                    Confounders

       (2) ✗      ╱            ╲
SNP ──(1)──▶ Exposure ─────────▶ Outcome
  ╲                                 ▲
   ╲───────────── (3) ✗ ────────────╱

  Relevance, because the SNP is only weakly linked to LDL-C
  Independence, because blood pressure confounds the SNP
  Exclusion restriction, through horizontal pleiotropy
  None, because this is vertical pleiotropy through LDL-C
  The SNP reaches CHD through a pathway (blood pressure) that bypasses LDL-C. That is horizontal pleiotropy, which violates the exclusion restriction.


  A SNP that explains very little of the exposure variance
  Allele frequency and outcome both differ between ancestries
  A SNP that affects the outcome through inflammation
  A SNP whose effect on the exposure is in SD units
  Population stratification links the SNP to confounders (ancestry-related factors), violating independence. A weak SNP is a relevance problem; an alternative pathway is an exclusion restriction problem.

text:
6.6 Multiple instruments, dose–response and pleiotropy
With several independent instruments, each shifting the exposure by a different amount, plot each SNP’s effect on the exposure (β-exposure, e.g. β-LDL-C) against its effect on the outcome (β-outcome, e.g. β-CHD). Example SNPs: SNP1 (LDLR), SNP2 (LDLR), SNP3 (PCSK9), SNP4 (APOE), SNP5 (APOB), all genes with known roles in LDL metabolism. A consistent dose–response line (larger effect on exposure → proportionally larger effect on outcome) strengthens confidence in causality.
Pleiotropy: one variant affecting more than one trait or pathway.










Vertical pleiotropy
Horizontal pleiotropy




Path
SNP affects the outcome via the exposure
SNP affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure


Example
SNP1 → PCSK9 → LDLR availability → LDL-C → atherosclerosis → CHD; or SNP2 → APOE → binding → same pathway
SNP3 → LDL-C → atherosclerosis → CHD, and SNP3 → inflammation → CHD


For MR
Not a problem: this is the causal chain MR is looking for
Bad: violates the exclusion restriction

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.7 The Wald ratio and IVW
One instrument: the Wald ratio
\[\hat\beta_{MR} = \frac{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to\text{outcome}}}{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to\text{exposure}}}\]
“Change in outcome per genetically predicted unit change in exposure.” If the outcome is binary, β-outcome must be on the log-odds scale. The three assumptions must still hold.
Many instruments. Compute a Wald ratio per instrument (after LD clumping), then combine. If instruments give noticeably different ratios, that disagreement is informative: horizontal pleiotropy in some instruments, or weak instruments.
Inverse-variance-weighted (IVW) MR, the standard way to combine: a linear regression of β-outcome on β-exposure across the instruments, through the origin, weighted by precision. Equivalent to a weighted average of the Wald ratios:
\[\hat\beta_{IVW} = \frac{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}\beta_{Y_j}\,/\,\sigma_{Y_j}^2}{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}^2\,/\,\sigma_{Y_j}^2}\]
where \(\beta_{X_j}\) is SNP \(j\)’s effect on the exposure, \(\beta_{Y_j}\) on the outcome, and \(\sigma_{Y_j}\) the SE of \(\beta_{Y_j}\). (The slides describe the weights as the precision of the estimates, “or a combined variance term”; the formula above is the standard first-order version.)
Outlier instruments, whose Wald ratio deviates from the rest, can arise from:

pleiotropy / a different biological pathway
measurement error
a weak instrument
population differences between the exposure and outcome studies
chance

Agreement strengthens confidence; strong disagreement motivates sensitivity analyses.

6.8 Sensitivity analyses: weighted median and MR-Egger











IVW
Weighted median
MR-Egger




Idea
Weighted regression through the origin = weighted mean of Wald ratios
Weighted median of the Wald ratios
Weighted regression with a free intercept


Valid if
All instruments valid (or pleiotropy balanced)
At least ~50% of the total instrument weight comes from valid instruments
Pleiotropic effects are independent of instrument strength (the InSIDE assumption; the slides do not use the acronym)

Nothing in particular

If IVW, weighted median and MR-Egger all point in a similar direction, confidence in causality increases substantially. The methods have different weaknesses, which are unlikely to all bias the result the same way.

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
text:
A genome-wide association study (GWAS) is one simple regression repeated about a million times. For each SNP you count how many copies of one allele each person carries (0, 1 or 2), regress the phenotype on that count, and record the effect size, its standard error and a p-value. That is the whole method; everything else in this lecture is about doing it carefully and reading the output correctly.
For example, if each copy of an allele raises LDL cholesterol by 0.2 mmol/L on average, the regression slope is 0.2. For a disease outcome you use logistic regression instead, and the slope becomes a log odds ratio.
The intuition to hold on to: genetic effects are usually small compared with everything else that varies between people, but with enough people you can still detect them. Testing a million SNPs at once also means you need a much stricter p-value threshold, and a significant SNP tells you where to look, not what is causal.
This page covers allele and genotype frequencies, the additive model for continuous and binary outcomes, covariates, GWAS summary statistics, multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots, why hits come in clusters, population structure and the step from a hit to biology. This lecture is calculation-heavy: be able to redo every worked example with new numbers.

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
section: 4.1 Genotype → phenotype, and why association is not causation
text:
4.1 Genotype → phenotype, and why association is not causation
DNA variation can plausibly cause a phenotype (disease status, a biomarker level). The reverse is logically impossible: a phenotype or disease cannot change your inherited DNA sequence, which was fixed at conception, long before any adult disease.
This directional certainty is exactly why genetic variants are useful for causal inference (Mendelian randomization, Lecture 6). But finding a variant associated with a phenotype is still only an association: confounding, chance and linkage can all produce a spurious-looking association, so causality still has to be investigated.

“Worth noting” 1: genetic effects are small. The spread of phenotype values within each dosage group (from all the non-genetic factors) is usually much larger than the difference between group means. With a large enough sample you still detect the signal. GWAS is not about finding “the one cause”; hits are clues pointing to proteins involved in physiology or disease.

Most GWAS use additive models because they test many SNPs at once and the additive model is the simplest, most tractable default that works reasonably across all of them. 4.5 Covariates
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 G + \beta_2 X_1 + \dots + \beta_n X_{n-1} + \varepsilon\]
\(G\) is genotype dosage; the \(X\)s are covariates such as age, sex, BMI and genetic principal components (PC1, PC2, …).
Why covariates are needed

Population structure. Allele frequency can differ between subpopulations, and the phenotype can also differ between them. Without adjustment you get a spurious SNP–phenotype association driven by structure, not biology (Section 4.9). The genetic principal components capture this.
Age, sex (and BMI). Often strong direct determinants of the phenotype. Adjusting removes their influence and reduces residual noise/confounding.
Technical variables. Genotyping batch, study center, or the batch/method used to measure the phenotype.

The same SNP can have a somewhat different β in two studies that adjusted for different covariates. When comparing effect estimates across papers, check what was adjusted for.

section: 4.7 Multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots
text:
4.7 Multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots
Testing ~1,000,000 SNPs at \(p < 0.05\) would give about \(1{,}000{,}000 \times 0.05 = 50{,}000\) false positives by chance. The field’s standard threshold is:
\[p < 5 \times 10^{-8} \approx \frac{0.05}{1{,}000{,}000}\]
a Bonferroni-style correction for ~1 million independent tests (Bonferroni is formalized in Lecture 7). Significance at this level means a SNP is statistically robust, not that it is biologically important or has a large effect.
Manhattan plot. x-axis: genomic position ordered by chromosome; y-axis: \(-\log_{10}(p)\), so stronger associations are taller (“skyscrapers”). Each dot is one SNP. Horizontal lines usually mark a suggestive threshold (~5×10⁻⁵ or similar) and genome-wide significance (5×10⁻⁸).





Simulated Manhattan plot. Three loci contain a true signal; LD makes each one a tower of neighbouring SNPs rather than a single point.










WarningTwo interpretive caveats (stated explicitly in the slides)




A Manhattan plot shows where the strongest associations are. It does not tell you which variant or gene is causal.
A low p-value does not mean a large effect. With a huge sample, even a tiny effect reaches genome-wide significance.



QQ plot. Observed p-values plotted against those expected under the null (no association anywhere). Points bending away from the diagonal more than chance predicts can signal a systematic problem (uncontrolled population structure, technical/batch artifacts). But it can also mean the trait is highly polygenic: very many small effects spread across the genome. That is the lecture’s explanation for LDL-C’s QQ plot looking “a bit off”: benign and expected for a polygenic trait.





Left: null SNPs follow the diagonal. Right: a polygenic trait (many small true effects) lifts the whole upper tail. Uncontrolled population structure can produce a similar lift, so the plot alone does not tell you which.





  The SNP must have a large effect on the phenotype
  The SNP is the causal variant at this locus
  The association is statistically robust, nothing more
  The SNP explains a large share of phenotype variance
  A tiny p-value in a huge sample only says the association is unlikely to be chance. Effect size, causality and variance explained are separate questions (see rs11591147 in Section 4.10).

text:
4.8 Why one signal gives a cluster: lead SNP and r²
Nearby SNPs are correlated (in LD) because they are inherited together. So one true causal variant appears as many associated SNPs: every SNP in LD with it shows an association, not because it is independently causal but because it is correlated. If two SNPs are in LD, knowing one tells you about the other. The result is one peak in the Manhattan plot.
From the cluster you pick a representative, the lead SNP: usually the one with the smallest p-value. The lead SNP is not guaranteed to be the causal variant; it may just be a good proxy.
Quantifying LD: \(r^2\), the squared correlation between two SNPs’ genotypes (0 to 1).

GWAS is a discovery tool. Causal inference needs extra assumptions and methods: Mendelian randomization (Lecture 6).

title: Lecture 2 — DNA, RNA and Protein
text:
Lecture 1 introduced the central dogma, DNA → RNA → protein, as a one-line idea. This lecture is the machinery behind that line: how a gene is copied into messenger RNA, how the ribosome reads that RNA three letters at a time, and how a protein comes out the other end.
Once you know how the machinery works, you can describe what happens when it goes wrong. A single changed letter can do nothing (a silent change), swap one amino acid (missense), or stop the protein early (nonsense). Inserting or deleting letters can shift how every following codon is read. These categories are the vocabulary for every mutation in the rest of the course, including the PCSK9 variant D374Y.
The key intuition is the reading frame: the ribosome reads mRNA in fixed groups of three. Most of the mutation rules follow from that one fact.
This page covers RNA vs DNA, transcription and strand terminology, translation and the genetic code, mutation types, the PCSK9 D374Y example and PCR. The strand-and-translate exercise at the bottom is the classic exam-style calculation.

2.2 Transcription, strands and directionality
Protein synthesis has two steps: transcription and translation. In transcription a gene (a defined stretch of DNA) is copied into mRNA; the mature mRNA is exported from the nucleus and translated in the cytoplasm.
Transcription factors are proteins that bind DNA and increase or decrease the rate of transcription. They are one of the main controls over which genes are “on” in which cell type.

DNA and RNA are always synthesized 5′ → 3′: new nucleotides are added to the 3′ end.
The new RNA strand is antiparallel to the DNA template strand. Antiparallel orientation is what makes base pairing physically possible.
DNA polymerase needs a primer to start. RNA polymerase does not.

text:
2.3 Translation and the genetic code
Translation: the ribosome reads the code in the mRNA and builds a protein. It takes place at ribosomes. The genetic code maps three-nucleotide codons to amino acids and has three properties:







Property
Meaning




Universal
Essentially the same in all known life


Unambiguous
Each codon specifies exactly one amino acid


Redundant (degenerate)
Most amino acids have several codons (64 codons, 20 amino acids)



tRNA’s role: each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that base-pairs with the matching codon, delivering the right amino acid at the right moment.
Three stages of translation

Initiation: the ribosome assembles on the mRNA at the start codon (AUG, methionine).
Elongation: amino acids are added one at a time as the ribosome moves along, each linked to the growing chain.
Termination: at a stop codon. The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA, given identically in Lectures 2 and 3. Memorize them.

Gene expression differs between cell types. Human cells have roughly 20,000 genes, but each cell type makes different proteins because different genes are expressed. Expression can be regulated at several stages:

chemical/structural modification of DNA or chromatin
transcription
post-transcriptional modification of RNA
mRNA degradation
post-translational modification of the protein

This is why having a gene and expressing it are different things, and why RNA and protein measurements depend on tissue and context (the layer table in Lecture 1).

Benjamini–Hochberg and Bonferroni side by side. Do several: the “largest k” rule and the running minimum for adjusted p-values are where mistakes happen.















TipBH checklist for the exam






Sort the p-values from smallest to largest; write the rank \(i\) next to each.
Compute the threshold \(\frac{i}{m} Q\) for every rank.
Find the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le \frac{i}{m} Q\). Call it \(k\). Do not stop at the first failure.
Everything with rank \(\le k\) is significant.
Adjusted p: compute \(p_{(i)} \cdot m / i\), then go from the bottom up taking the running minimum. Cap at 1.
Bonferroni for comparison: one threshold \(\alpha/m\) (or \(p \times m\)), same for all.
State the interpretation: BH controls the FDR (expected share of false hits among hits); Bonferroni controls the FWER (probability of any false hit).

title: Exam practice
text:
🎯 Lecture 7: high-dimensional data






TipQ1. Explain why the ordinary t-test is problematic for omics data with few samples, and how the moderated t-statistic solves it.





Model answer. In omics data we measure thousands of features on few replicates, e.g. 3 vs 3 samples, giving only \(n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 4\) degrees of freedom per feature. Each feature’s variance \(s^2\) is estimated separately and is therefore very unstable. By chance some features get a tiny \(s^2\); since \(s^2\) is in the denominator of \(t\), they get huge t-values although the mean difference is small → false positives. Others get a randomly large \(s^2\), masking real effects → lost power. This instability affects every p-value and so also undermines the multiple-testing correction.
The moderated t (limma, empirical Bayes) shares information across all features: each variance is shrunk toward a common variance \(s_0^2\) estimated from the whole dataset, \(\tilde s^2 = (d_0 s_0^2 + d\, s^2)/(d_0 + d)\). With few replicates the prior weight \(d_0\) dominates and the shrinkage is strong; with many replicates the feature’s own variance dominates. Result: fewer false positives, more power, more reliable FDR-adjusted results. → 7.7–7.8









TipQ2. Define FWER and FDR. Which correction methods control each, and which is preferred for a miRNA microarray screen? Give reasons.





Model answer. FWER = P(at least one false positive among all tests), controlled by Bonferroni (\(p \le \alpha/m\)). FDR = the expected proportion of false positives among all tests called significant, E[FP / positives], controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg.
For omics screens FDR/BH is preferred: (1) with thousands of tests Bonferroni’s threshold is so small that most true effects are missed (0.05/955 ≈ 0.00005); (2) the analysis is exploratory, producing a shortlist where a controlled fraction of false leads is acceptable; (3) hits are validated afterwards in an independent cohort/method (miR-375 by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization); (4) features are correlated, so the effective number of tests is smaller than \(m\) and Bonferroni is needlessly strict. → 7.11–7.14









TipQ3. The study tested 955 miRNAs. How many significant results would you expect at p < 0.05 if no miRNA truly differed? What is the Bonferroni threshold?





Model answer. \(955 \times 0.05 \approx 48\) false positives. Bonferroni: \(0.05/955 \approx 5.2 \times 10^{-5}\) (≈ 0.00005). With 955 independent null tests the chance of at least one false positive is \(1 - 0.95^{955} \approx 1\), so the cutoff itself must change. → 7.10









TipQ4. Describe the preprocessing of the microarray data. What does quantile normalization do and what does it assume?





Model answer. Observed signal = biological signal + technical noise (RNA extraction, labelling, hybridization, scanner, batch). Steps: (1) quality control; (2) background correction within each array with normexp, which models observed = signal (exponential) + background (normal) and estimates the true signal, giving positive values and better low-intensity estimates; (3) normalization between arrays with quantile normalization: rank the values in each array, average across arrays at each rank, replace each value by its rank mean, so all arrays get an identical distribution while keeping each array’s internal order; (4) average replicate probes (4–8 spots) per miRNA. Assumption of quantile normalization: the overall expression distribution should be the same in every sample, so distribution differences are technical. → 7.4–7.5









TipQ5. The authors clustered the samples on miRNA expression, found clusters M1 and M2, and then reported 141 miRNAs differentially expressed between M1 and M2. Comment critically.





Model answer. This is circular reasoning: the clusters were defined from the same miRNA data that was then tested. Clustering produces groups that differ in the clustering variables almost by construction, so significant differences are expected even in pure noise and the p-values are inflated. The differences are not independent evidence. Valid alternatives: test the cluster–clinical associations (grade, Ki67, chromosome 14 gain, which used other data), validate the clusters in an independent cohort, or use methods that account for the selection. → 7.16b









TipQ6. What does log₂FC = 1.5 mean? And why log-transform expression data at all?





Model answer. \(2^{1.5} \approx 2.83\): expression is about 2.8 times higher in the first group. log₂FC = 0 means no change, +1 twice as high, −1 half as high. Log₂ transformation makes the distribution more symmetric and reduces the influence of very large raw values; on the log scale, fold changes become differences. → 7.9









TipQ7. Five patients had both a primary tumour and a liver metastasis. Why were only their primary tumours used in the tumour vs normal comparison?





Model answer. Two samples from the same patient are not independent. Including both would double-weight those patients and violate the independence assumption of the test, biasing variance estimates and p-values. → 7.9b

title: Exam practice
text:
📌 Lectures 4–6: GWAS and Mendelian randomization






TipQ8. State the three assumptions of Mendelian randomization and give a threat to each.





Model answer. 1. Relevance: the variant is robustly associated with the exposure (genome-wide significant). Threat: weak instruments, which bias and destabilize the estimate. 2. Independence: the variant is not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship. Threats: population stratification, assortative mating, selection effects. 3. Exclusion restriction: the variant affects the outcome only through the exposure. Threat: horizontal pleiotropy (another pathway, e.g. SNP → inflammation → CHD). → 6.5









TipQ9. Distinguish vertical and horizontal pleiotropy. Which one is a problem for MR and why?





Model answer. Vertical: the SNP affects the outcome through the exposure (SNP → PCSK9 → LDLR → LDL-C → CHD); this is the causal chain MR measures, not a problem. Horizontal: the SNP also affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure (SNP → inflammation → CHD); this violates the exclusion restriction and biases the MR estimate, because part of the SNP–outcome association is wrongly attributed to the exposure. → 6.6









TipQ10. Explain the Wald ratio, IVW, weighted median and MR-Egger. When would you trust a causal conclusion?





Model answer. Wald ratio (one instrument): \(\beta_{\text{outcome}}/\beta_{\text{exposure}}\), change in outcome per genetically predicted unit of exposure (log-odds for binary outcomes). IVW: weighted regression of β-outcome on β-exposure through the origin = precision-weighted average of the Wald ratios; assumes all instruments valid. Weighted median: consistent if at least ~50% of the instrument weight is valid, so robust to a minority of bad instruments. MR-Egger: free intercept; a non-zero intercept indicates directional horizontal pleiotropy; less precise and more sensitive to weak instruments, relies on the InSIDE assumption. Trust grows when all methods point in the same direction, since their weaknesses differ. Always state the exposure unit and the direction. → 6.7–6.9









TipQ11. Why are genetic variants useful for causal inference? Compare MR with an RCT.





Model answer. Genotype is fixed at conception, so it precedes the disease: no reverse causation. Alleles are allocated randomly at meiosis, like treatment in an RCT, so they are (under the independence assumption) unrelated to confounders such as smoking. An allele that lowers LDL-C is a lifelong “natural trial” of lower LDL-C. MR is cheaper and possible where RCTs are not, but relies on the three instrument assumptions. → 6.3–6.4









TipQ12. A Manhattan plot shows a tall peak with dozens of significant SNPs. Explain why, and what “lead SNP” and “locus” mean. Is the lead SNP causal?





Model answer. Nearby SNPs are correlated (in LD) because they are inherited together, so one causal variant makes all SNPs in LD with it look associated. The locus is the region containing the associated signal; the lead SNP is the one with the smallest p-value there. It is not necessarily causal: it may be a proxy, and the causal variant may not even be on the array. Ways forward: conditional analysis, credible sets, functional annotation, protein folding models, pQTL evidence, experiments (knock-in mice). → 4.8, 5.3–5.4









TipQ13. What is population stratification and how is it handled in a GWAS?





Model answer. If allele frequencies and the phenotype both differ between ancestry groups, pooling them creates a spurious SNP–phenotype association even without any biological effect. Handling: restrict to genetically homogeneous ancestry groups; adjust for genetic principal components; use mixed models that account for relatedness (e.g. regenie); check the QQ plot and genomic inflation. → 4.9









TipQ14. Why is the genome-wide significance threshold 5×10⁻⁸? Does p < 5×10⁻⁸ mean the SNP matters?





Model answer. About 1 million independent tests: \(0.05/10^6 = 5 \times 10^{-8}\) (Bonferroni); at 0.05 you would get ~50,000 false positives. Significance means statistical robustness only. It says nothing about effect size (huge samples make tiny effects significant), causality or public-health relevance (rs11591147 has a big effect but is rare, 1.5%). → 4.7, 4.10









TipQ15. What must you always know when using GWAS summary statistics?





Model answer. Which allele is the effect allele (A1/EA); whether β is an OR or log(OR) for binary outcomes; the scale of the phenotype (log? SD units?); the genome build (GRCh37/hg19 vs GRCh38). When combining datasets also check SNP coverage, allele/strand alignment and ancestry of the LD reference panel. rsIDs help avoid mismatches. → 4.6, 5.6









TipQ16. List the Bradford Hill criteria.





Model answer. Strength, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological gradient (dose–response), Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment, Analogy. → 6.2

title: Exam practice
text:
📌 Lectures 1–3: biology and genetics






TipQ17. Explain the LDLR–PCSK9–LDL-C pathway, and how Leqvio and Repatha lower LDL-C differently.





Model answer. The LDL receptor on hepatocytes clears LDL from the blood. PCSK9 promotes LDLR degradation, so more PCSK9 → fewer receptors → higher LDL-C → more atherosclerosis. Leqvio (inclisiran) is an siRNA linked to GalNAc, which binds ASGPR on liver cells; inside, it degrades PCSK9 mRNA, so less PCSK9 is made. Repatha/Praluent are monoclonal antibodies binding free PCSK9 protein in blood, blocking its action. Both leave more LDLR and lower LDL-C: two druggable points on one pathway. D374Y (GoF) raises LDL-C; PCSK9 LoF lowers it, as the drugs mimic. → 1.2, 3.2b, 3.3









TipQ18. Compare germline and somatic mutations.





Model answer. Germline: arise in egg/sperm, present in every cell, heritable, detected in blood/saliva, cause inherited disorders and hereditary cancer syndromes. Somatic: acquired during life in non-reproductive cells, confined to the tissue/tumour, not heritable, need a biopsy of the tissue, drive cancers and benign tumours (e.g. AML, detected by targeted deep sequencing and VAF). → 3.4









TipQ19. Read this variant: NM_174936.4(PCSK9):c.1120G>T, p.Asp374Tyr, rs137852912.





Model answer. In PCSK9 transcript NM_174936 version 4 (NM_ = mRNA reference), coding DNA position 1120 has G replaced by T. At the protein level (p.) aspartic acid 374 becomes tyrosine (D374Y): a missense, gain-of-function SNV. rs137852912 is its dbSNP identifier; its genomic position is chr1:55057454 in GRCh38 and 55523127 in GRCh37 (NC_ prefix, g. coordinates). → 3.3b–3.3c









TipQ20. Compare miRNA and siRNA.





Model answer. miRNA: ~22 nt, genome-encoded, binds targets imperfectly, inhibits translation or promotes degradation, regulates many mRNAs (why it is widely dysregulated in cancer). siRNA: ~21–23 nt, from double-stranded RNA, binds with near-perfect complementarity, cleaves one specific mRNA, used as designed drugs (Leqvio). → 3.2









TipQ21. Define linkage, recombination frequency and linkage disequilibrium. How is LD detected?





Model answer. Linkage: loci close on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. Recombination frequency \(r\) = recombinant offspring / total, 0% (complete linkage) to 50% (unlinked). LD: non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population. Detected by comparing observed haplotype frequency with the expected product of allele frequencies (e.g. expected AB = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20); a difference indicates LD. Quantified with \(r^2\) (> 0.8 very strong; < 0.01 treated as independent). → 3.7









TipQ22. Give the five categories of biomarker with an example each. Is a biomarker causal?





Model answer. Exposure (cotinine for tobacco), biological process (CRP for inflammation), disease/tissue injury (troponin for myocardial injury), future risk (LDL-C for atherosclerosis), treatment response (LDL-C change on lipid-lowering therapy). Being a biomarker does not imply causality. → 1.3b

title: Exam practice
text:
📌 Lecture 8: proteomics






TipQ23. What is a cis-pQTL vs a trans-pQTL, and why are cis-pQTLs preferred as MR instruments?





Model answer. A pQTL is a SNP associated with a protein’s abundance. cis: near the encoding gene (mechanisms: transcription, splicing, stability, secretion). trans: far away, > 500 kb or another chromosome (mechanisms: transcription factors, receptors, signalling). cis-pQTLs are preferred because the link to the protein is direct and there is less risk of horizontal pleiotropy; they still need all three MR assumptions. Protein MR: \(\beta_{MR} = \beta_{GO}/\beta_{GP}\). → 8.9–8.10









TipQ24. List challenges specific to protein MR.





Model answer. Horizontal pleiotropy (especially trans-pQTLs); assay binding artifacts (coding variants change the epitope, fake lower abundance); amount ≠ function (variants changing activity without abundance are invisible); LD creating false appearance of causality (different SNPs in LD for protein and disease), checked by colocalization; one pQTL affecting several proteins. → 8.11









TipQ25. How do you prevent and correct batch effects in a large proteomics study?





Model answer. Batch = plate, reagent lot, run, day, instrument, operator. Prevent (design): randomize samples across plates, balance cases and controls, technical replicates across plates, common reference samples on every plate. Detect: boxplots by plate, PCA, clustering, controls, replicates. Correct (analysis): normalization across plates/batches (incl. reference-sample normalization), adjust for plate/run or include batch as a covariate. Also consider pre-analytical variation (fasting, time to centrifugation, freeze–thaw, hemolysis) that may differ systematically between cases and controls. → 8.6









TipQ26. Compare the three families of protein measurement technology.





Model answer. Antibody-based (ELISA, immunoassays, Western blot): targeted, quantitative with standards, clinical routine. Mass spectrometry: trypsin digestion → LC → electrospray → masses; detects isoforms, allows discovery; complex, dynamic-range problems, labelled peptides for calibration. High-throughput affinity (Olink, SomaScan): thousands of proteins in large cohorts (UKBB: ~50,000 people, ~3,000 proteins), relative abundance in NPX (log₂; 1 NPX = doubling). → 8.4–8.5

A1. PLINK 2 files and genotype QC
PLINK 2 stores a genotype dataset as three files with the same name:







File
Contents

The genotype matrix itself (every individual × every variant), in a compact binary format


.pvar
One row per variant: chromosome, position, ID (rsID), reference and alternative allele. .pvar.zst is a compressed version (read with vzs)

QC filters and why they are used








PLINK flag
Keeps
Why

Single-nucleotide variants with plain A/C/G/T alleles
Drops indels and odd allele codes that complicate matching between datasets

Biallelic variants
The additive 0/1/2 model assumes exactly two alleles

  An unusual share of people had many missing genotype calls

section: A2. Why rare variants are hard for single-SNP regression
text:
A2. Why rare variants are hard for single-SNP regression
The standard error of the per-allele β shrinks with the number of carriers. For a continuous phenotype with residual SD \(\sigma\) and \(n\) people, approximately
\[\text{SE}(\hat\beta) \approx \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\,n\,\text{MAF}\,(1-\text{MAF})}}\]
because the variance of the 0/1/2 dosage under HWE is \(2\,\text{MAF}(1-\text{MAF})\). With MAF = 0.001 in 2,500 people you expect only about 5 carriers, so β rests on a handful of people: huge SE, low power, and sensitivity to a single genotyping error.





Approximate SE of β (phenotype SD = 1) against MAF, for 2,500 and 100,000 people. SE explodes as MAF approaches zero; the dashed line marks MAF = 0.01.

text:
A4. Significant SNP, lead SNP, independent signal







Term
What it is




Significant SNP
Any SNP with p below the threshold (e.g. 5×10⁻⁸). Many can come from one causal variant


Lead SNP
The strongest (smallest p) SNP in a region; the representative of a peak


Independent signal
What is left after clumping: lead SNPs with r² below the threshold (e.g. < 0.01) to each other


Causal SNP
The variant that actually changes biology. It may be a lead SNP, a SNP in LD with it, or not genotyped at all



Does distance predict LD? Only roughly. LD tends to decay with distance, but recombination hotspots, allele frequencies and population history make the relationship very noisy. Always compute r².

title: Computer exercises: concepts
text:
A5. Manual LD clumping
The algorithm used in the exercises:

Among the remaining significant SNPs, pick the smallest p-value as a lead SNP.
Compute r² between it and every other remaining significant SNP.
Remove all SNPs with r² ≥ 0.01 (they are “the same signal”).
Keep the lead as one signal and repeat from step 1 until nothing is left.

Practise on invented tables. The drill gives a new table each time.












TipCommon mistakes in clumping






Starting from a SNP that is not the strongest remaining one.
Comparing with SNPs that have already been removed.
Using a threshold in the wrong direction (remove r² ≥ 0.01, keep r² < 0.01).
Concluding that the lead SNPs are causal. They are the strongest statistical signals. A simulated phenotype, where the causal SNPs are known, is exactly the situation where you can check this.

Summary statistics have one row per SNP and no individual genotypes, so the correlation between two SNPs (LD) cannot be computed from them. You need a reference panel with individual-level genotypes, e.g. 1000 Genomes, from a population with matching ancestry, because LD patterns differ between populations. → 5.5

Instruments must be independent, or the same signal is counted several times
5.4b


Look up the lead SNPs in the outcome GWAS
Need βoutcome for each instrument; missing SNPs are lost (or replaced by proxies)
6.1


Align alleles
βexposure and βoutcome must refer to the same allele
B2 above


Wald ratio per SNP; IVW, MR-Egger, weighted median
Estimate and check robustness
6.7, 6.8



A common convention is to orient every SNP so that the effect allele raises the exposure (βexposure > 0), flipping both betas when needed. The MR scatter plot then lies in the right half.

section: C2. Reading an MR analysis: a simulated example
text:
C2. Reading an MR analysis: a simulated example
Simulated data, not the course data: 30 independent instruments with a true causal effect of 0.5 (log-odds of the outcome per unit exposure). Four instruments also have a direct effect on the outcome (horizontal pleiotropy).





Simulated MR scatter. Orange points are the four pleiotropic instruments. IVW (green) is forced through the origin; MR-Egger (orange, dashed) has a free intercept; the dotted line shows the true effect 0.5.







MR estimates for the simulated data (true causal effect = 0.5)


Method
Estimate
p-value




IVW
0.543
2.3e-15


MR-Egger (slope)
0.335
8.4e-05


MR-Egger (intercept)
0.031
0.004


Weighted median
0.505
n/a





How to read it

IVW uses all instruments and assumes they are all valid. With positive pleiotropy in a few SNPs it is pulled upward.
Weighted median is robust as long as at least ~50% of the weight comes from valid instruments. Here it should be closer to 0.5.
MR-Egger’s intercept estimates the average pleiotropic effect. Here it is clearly non-zero, signalling directional pleiotropy. The Egger slope is meant to be the pleiotropy-adjusted estimate, but in this simulation it lands well below the truth: with only four pleiotropic SNPs among 30, the free intercept over-corrects. Egger is imprecise and relies on its own assumption (InSIDE), so treat its slope as a sensitivity check, not the answer.
Agreement in direction across the three methods supports a causal effect; the size of the estimates should be interpreted with the exposure unit in mind (6.9).


  Consistent evidence of a positive effect, no sign of directional pleiotropy
  The Egger intercept shows strong pleiotropy, so IVW is invalid
  The methods disagree in direction, so no conclusion is possible
  The effect is negative, since Egger’s slope is smaller than IVW
  All three estimates are positive and similar, and the Egger intercept is close to zero and non-significant. That is the triangulation pattern that strengthens a causal interpretation. The Egger p-value is larger simply because Egger is less precise.


  A strong and robust causal effect, since IVW is the main method
  IVW is probably driven by pleiotropic instruments; be cautious
  The weighted median is wrong because its p-value is not significant
  Egger’s intercept confirms that the instruments are all valid
  The robust method (weighted median) finds almost nothing, and the Egger intercept indicates directional pleiotropy. IVW, which assumes all instruments are valid, is then likely biased. Look for outlying instruments and do not claim causality from IVW alone.


  Nothing, because IVW only uses βexposure
  Those five points land on the wrong side of the line
  All points move closer to the origin by the same amount
  The Wald ratios of those five SNPs become exactly zero
  A swapped allele gives the outcome β the wrong sign, so those SNPs point in the opposite direction from the rest. They pull IVW toward zero and can create a spurious Egger intercept. This is why allele alignment comes before any MR estimate.

title: Glossary
text:
A–C

Additive model

The standard GWAS model: phenotype regressed on allele dosage (0/1/2), so each extra copy adds the same effect β. Additive/dominant/recessive describe the genotype–phenotype relationship, not the allele. L4 §4.4

Allele

An alternative version (DNA sequence) at a particular locus. L3 §3.6 · L4 §4.2

Allele frequency / MAF

How common an allele is in a population. MAF (minor allele frequency) is the frequency of the less common allele. L4 §4.2

Alternative splicing

One gene’s transcript spliced into several different mRNA/protein variants; one reason proteins are not 1-to-1 with genes. L8 §8.1

AML (acute myeloid leukemia)

A non-solid blood cancer driven by somatic mutations in bone marrow stem cells; the course’s example of somatic mutation diagnostics with NGS and VAF. L3 §3.4

Antibody-based assay

ELISA, clinical immunoassays, Western blot: an antibody binds its target protein; targeted and quantitative with calibration standards. L8 §8.4

Assay binding artifact

A coding variant changes the protein’s structure so the antibody/aptamer binds worse, giving a falsely low measured level. A protein-MR pitfall. L8 §8.11

Assortative mating

Non-random mate choice related to a trait; a threat to the MR independence assumption. L6 §6.5

Background correction (normexp)

Within-array correction modelling observed intensity as exponential signal + normal background noise; gives positive values and better low-intensity estimates. L7 §7.5

Batch effect

A shared technical artifact among samples processed together (plate, reagent lot, run, day, instrument, operator). Prevent by randomizing/balancing; correct by normalization or batch covariates. L7 §7.4 · L8 §8.6

Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)

FDR-controlling procedure: sort p-values, find the largest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ (k/m)Q, call ranks 1…k significant. Adjusted p = running minimum of p₍ᵢ₎·m/i from the bottom. L7 §7.13 · L7 §7.13b

Biomarker

Any measurable biological characteristic informative about a process, exposure, disease or treatment response. Five roles: exposure, process, disease/injury, future risk, treatment response. Not necessarily causal. L1 §1.3b

Bonferroni correction

FWER control: reject if p ≤ α/m (p_adj = p × m). Valid under any dependence but very strict for large m. L7 §7.12 · L4 §4.7

Bradford Hill criteria

Strength, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological gradient, Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment, Analogy. L6 §6.2

Central dogma

The flow of genetic information DNA → RNA → protein. L1 §1.4 · L2 §2.2

Chromosomal alterations

Large-scale changes: deletion, duplication, inversion, insertion, translocation. L2 §2.4b

Circular reasoning (double dipping)

Using the same data to define groups (e.g. clusters) and then to test differences between those groups; inflates significance. L7 §7.16b

cis-pQTL

A pQTL located near the gene encoding the protein; direct interpretation, preferred MR instrument. L8 §8.9 · L4 §4.10

Codon

Three nucleotides specifying one amino acid (or stop). 64 codons for 20 amino acids. L1 §1.4b · L2 §2.3

Coding strand

The non-template DNA strand; same sequence as the mRNA with T instead of U. L2 §2.2

Colocalization

Checks whether a pQTL and a disease GWAS signal at one locus share the same causal variant by comparing their association patterns across the region. L8 §8.11

Complementary base pairing

A pairs with T (U in RNA), C pairs with G; the basis of replication and transcription. L1 §1.4b

Conditional analysis

Adding the lead SNP as a covariate and retesting other SNPs to find independent signals. L5 §5.4

Confounding

A third factor affecting both exposure and outcome (e.g. smoking → LDL-C and CHD). L6 §6.4 · L8 §8.8

Covariates (in GWAS)

Age, sex, BMI, genetic PCs, technical variables (batch, center). β is conditional on them. L4 §4.5

Credible set

A set of candidate causal SNPs chosen from association strength and LD structure. L5 §5.4

title: Glossary
text:
D–H

dbSNP / rs number

NCBI database of short variants; each gets a stable rs identifier (e.g. rs137852912 = PCSK9 D374Y). L3 §3.3c

Dominant / recessive allele

Dominant affects the phenotype with at least one copy; recessive only with two. L3 §3.6

Empirical Bayes / variance shrinkage

Sharing information across features: each variance is pulled toward a common value. Basis of limma’s moderated t. L7 §7.7 · L7 §7.8

Exclusion restriction

MR assumption 3: the variant affects the outcome only through the exposure. Broken by horizontal pleiotropy. L6 §6.5

FDR (false discovery rate)

Expected proportion of false positives among the tests called significant. Controlled by BH. L7 §7.11

Frameshift

An indel whose length is not a multiple of 3, shifting all downstream codons. L2 §2.4b

FWER (family-wise error rate)

Probability of at least one false positive among all tests. Controlled by Bonferroni. L7 §7.11

Gain / loss of function (GoF / LoF)

A mutation making the protein work better (D374Y in PCSK9) or worse (p.Tyr142*, p.Arg97del). L3 §3.3

GalNAc / ASGPR

Sugar linked to the siRNA in Leqvio that binds ASGPR receptors on hepatocytes: an “address label” to the liver. L3 §3.2b

Gene expression

Transcription + translation; regulated at chromatin, transcription, RNA processing, mRNA degradation and post-translational levels. L1 §1.4 · L2 §2.3

Genome build (GRCh37/hg19, GRCh38)

Versions of the human reference genome; the same variant has different coordinates in different builds. HG18/HG19 are older names. L3 §3.3c · L4 §4.6

Genome-wide significance

p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ ≈ 0.05 / 1,000,000. L4 §4.7

Genotype / phenotype

Genotype = the alleles an individual carries; phenotype = the observable trait. L3 §3.6

Genotyping

Determining alleles at already-known variant positions (TaqMan, SNP arrays), as opposed to sequencing. L3 §3.5 · L3 §3.8

Germline mutation

Arises in germ cells, present in every cell, heritable. L3 §3.4

GWAS

Genome-wide association study: one regression per SNP for ~1 million SNPs. Gives associations, not causality. L3 §3.8 · L4 §4.6 · L5 §5.2

Haplotype

A combination of alleles at two or more loci on the same chromosome copy. L3 §3.7

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)

With allele frequencies p and q: P(AA) = p², P(Aa) = 2pq, P(aa) = q². Deviations are a genotyping QC check. L3 §3.9 · L4 §4.2

HGVS nomenclature

Standard variant notation: reference (NM_ mRNA, NC_ genomic, NP_ protein) + coordinate type (c., g., p.) + change (e.g. c.1120G>T, p.Asp374Tyr). L3 §3.3b

Homozygous / heterozygous

Two identical alleles (BB, bb) vs two different alleles (Bb). L3 §3.6

Horizontal pleiotropy

A variant affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure; violates the exclusion restriction. L6 §6.6 · L8 §8.11

title: Glossary
text:
I–M

Imputation

Predicting genotypes at unmeasured SNPs from measured SNPs using LD and a reference panel. L6 §6.1

In-frame indel

An insertion/deletion of a multiple of 3 nucleotides; frame preserved (e.g. PCSK9 p.Arg97del). L2 §2.4b

Independence (MR assumption)

MR assumption 2: the variant is not associated with confounders. Threats: population stratification, assortative mating, selection. L6 §6.5

Instrumental variable

A variable affecting the exposure but related to the outcome only through it; genetic variants are natural instruments. L6 §6.3

IVW (inverse-variance weighted) MR

Weighted regression of β-outcome on β-exposure through the origin = weighted average of Wald ratios. L6 §6.7

LD clumping

Reducing each locus to one approximately independent lead SNP (e.g. r² < 0.01); done before MR. L5 §5.4b

LDL / LDLR

Low-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol; the LDL receptor on hepatocytes clears it. L1 §1.2

Lead SNP

The SNP with the smallest p-value in a locus; not necessarily causal. L4 §4.8 · L5 §5.3

limma / moderated t-statistic

R package using empirical Bayes variance shrinkage to give stable t-statistics with few samples. L7 §7.7

Linkage

Loci close on the same chromosome are inherited together. L3 §3.7

Linkage disequilibrium (LD)

Non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population; observed ≠ expected haplotype frequency. Measured by r² (or D). L3 §3.7 · L4 §4.8

Locus

A position on a chromosome; in GWAS, a region containing associated variants (one Manhattan peak). L3 §3.6 · L4 §4.10

Log₂ fold change

log₂(group 1 / group 2): 0 = no change, +1 = 2× higher, −1 = 2× lower. L7 §7.9

Manhattan plot

−log₁₀(p) against genomic position; peaks show where associations are, not which variant is causal. L4 §4.7

Mass spectrometry

Trypsin digestion → liquid chromatography → electrospray ionization → mass measurement; detects isoforms, allows discovery. L8 §8.4

Meiosis / mitosis

Meiosis: 4 different gametes with 23 chromosomes. Mitosis: 2 identical cells with 46. L1 §1.4c

Mendel’s laws

Dominance, Segregation, Independent Assortment (broken by linkage). L3 §3.6

Mendelian randomization (MR)

Using genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects of an exposure on an outcome. L6 §6.3 · L8 §8.10

Metabolite

A small molecule produced, modified or consumed in biochemical reactions (e.g. glucose). L1 §1.3

miRNA (microRNA)

~22 nt genome-encoded non-coding RNA; binds targets imperfectly and regulates many mRNAs. L3 §3.2 · L7 §7.2

Missense / nonsense / silent

Substitution giving a different amino acid / a premature stop / the same amino acid. L2 §2.4

Monoclonal antibody

An engineered protein binding one specific target; Repatha and Praluent bind PCSK9 protein. L3 §3.2b

MR-Egger

MR regression with a free intercept; a non-zero intercept signals directional horizontal pleiotropy. Less precise than IVW. L6 §6.8

mRNA / rRNA / tRNA

Messenger RNA carries the code; ribosomal RNA builds ribosomes; transfer RNA brings amino acids. L2 §2.1

Multiple testing

Many tests at α = 0.05 give many false positives (955 × 0.05 ≈ 48; 1,000,000 × 0.05 = 50,000). L7 §7.10 · L4 §4.7

title: Glossary
text:
N–R

NGS (next-generation sequencing)

Massively parallel sequencing: fast and cheap, short reads (~50–300 nt). L3 §3.5

NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression)

Olink/SomaScan relative abundance on a log₂ scale; 1 NPX = a doubling. L8 §8.5

Olink / SomaScan

High-throughput affinity proteomics platforms for large cohorts. L8 §8.4

OncomiR

A miRNA that promotes cancer (e.g. miR-1246, miR-663a). L7 §7.2 · L7 §7.16

Odds ratio (per allele)

OR = exp(β) from logistic regression; β = −0.16 → OR 0.85 (one copy), 0.73 (two copies). L4 §4.3

PCR

Polymerase chain reaction: in vitro amplification of a DNA region using heat-stable Taq polymerase and primers. L2 §2.6

PCSK9

Protein promoting LDLR degradation; the course’s running drug-target example. L1 §1.2 · L3 §3.3 · L8 §8.12

Population stratification

Allele frequency and phenotype both differ between ancestry groups, creating spurious associations. L4 §4.9

Pre-analytical variation

Variation before the assay: fasting, time of day, tube type, time to centrifugation, storage, freeze–thaw, hemolysis. L8 §8.6

Primer

Short DNA sequence where synthesis starts; DNA polymerase needs one, RNA polymerase does not. L2 §2.2 · L2 §2.6

Protein structure (4 levels)

Primary (sequence), secondary (helices, sheets), tertiary (3D fold), quaternary (several chains). L1 §1.4

Proteome

All proteins in a sample; more dynamic and complex than the genome. L8 §8.1

Proxy SNP

A SNP in very strong LD (r² ≈ 1) that stands in for a missing SNP. L6 §6.1

Post-translational modification (PTM)

Chemical changes after translation, e.g. phosphorylation, glycosylation, cleavage. L8 §8.1

pQTL (protein quantitative trait locus)

A SNP associated with a protein’s abundance; cis (near the gene) or trans (> 500 kb away). L8 §8.9

PWAS

Proteome-wide association study: one regression per protein. L8 §8.7

QQ plot

Observed vs expected p-values; deviation can mean confounding/batch or high polygenicity. L4 §4.7

QTL

Quantitative trait locus: a region where genetic variation is associated with a quantitative trait (expression, protein, metabolite). L4 §4.10

Quantile normalization

Between-array normalization making all distributions identical while keeping within-array order. L7 §7.5

r² (LD)

Squared genotype correlation between two SNPs: > 0.8 very strong, > 0.5 moderate–strong, < 0.1 weak, ≈ 0 independent. L4 §4.8 · L5 §5.4b

Recombination / recombination frequency

Exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in meiosis; r = recombinants / total, 0–50%. L3 §3.7

Relevance (MR assumption)

MR assumption 1: the variant is strongly associated with the exposure; threat: weak instruments. L6 §6.5

title: Glossary
text:
S–Z

Sanger sequencing

The original sequencing method: accurate, lower throughput. L3 §3.5

siRNA

~21–23 nt RNA from double-stranded RNA; near-perfect match cleaves one target mRNA (Leqvio). L3 §3.2

SNP / SNV

Single nucleotide variant; called a SNP (polymorphism) when common in the population. L2 §2.4 · L4 §4.2

SNP array

Chip with allele-specific probes genotyping up to millions of known SNPs by hybridization and fluorescence. L3 §3.8

snRNA

Small nuclear RNA involved in splicing. L3 §3.1

Somatic mutation

Acquired during life, confined to a tissue, not heritable. L3 §3.4

Summary statistics

Per-SNP GWAS results (SNP, CHR, BP, A1, A2, EAF, β, SE, P, N) with no individual-level data. L4 §4.6

Supervised / unsupervised analysis

Using predefined group labels (differential expression) vs finding groups from the data (clustering). L7 §7.6

Taq polymerase

Heat-stable DNA polymerase used in PCR. L2 §2.6

Template strand

The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase (non-coding strand). L2 §2.2

Transcription / translation

DNA → mRNA (in the nucleus) / mRNA → protein at the ribosome (initiation, elongation, termination at UAA, UAG, UGA). L2 §2.2 · L2 §2.3

Transcription factor

Protein binding DNA to raise or lower transcription. L2 §2.2

trans-pQTL

pQTL far (> 500 kb or other chromosome) from the encoding gene; indirect, more pleiotropy risk. L8 §8.9

Troponin

Released by damaged heart muscle; a marker of injury, predictive but not causal. L1 §1.3b · L8 §8.8

VAF (variant allele frequency)

Fraction of reads/cells in one patient’s sample carrying a mutation. L3 §3.4

Vertical pleiotropy

The variant affects the outcome through the exposure itself; not a problem for MR. L6 §6.6

Wald ratio

MR estimate with one instrument: β_outcome / β_exposure (β_GO / β_GP in protein MR). L6 §6.7 · L8 §8.10

Weighted median

MR estimator valid if at least ~50% of instrument weight is valid. L6 §6.8

z-score

(x − mean) / SD; puts proteins on a common scale, β per SD. L8 §8.6 · L8 §8.7

title: Lecture 1 — The Biological Language of Molecular Epidemiology
text:
Molecular epidemiology is epidemiology that looks inside the body. Classical epidemiology links an exposure (smoking, diet, a drug) to a disease and treats everything in between as a black box. Molecular epidemiology opens that box. It measures DNA variants, RNA levels, proteins and metabolites across many people and asks how they relate to exposures and disease.
The course runs on one clinical example: a young patient with a heart attack, a father who had one too, and very high LDL cholesterol in the whole family. Following that family from DNA to protein to blood lipids to heart disease introduces almost every idea in the course, and the same LDLR/PCSK9 pathway comes back in Lectures 2, 3, 6 and 8.
The key intuition is that a molecule linked to a disease can play three roles. It can cause the disease, it can reflect a disease process that is already running, or it can simply be associated with it through something else. Most of the course is about telling these three apart.
This page covers the framing of the field, the LDL/PCSK9 example, the molecular measurement layers and biomarker types, and the DNA and protein structure you need for everything after this.

title: Lecture 1 — The Biological Language of Molecular Epidemiology
text:
1.1 What molecular epidemiology actually is
Classical epidemiology asks whether an exposure (smoking, diet, a drug) is associated with a disease outcome in a population and usually treats the biology in between as a black box. Molecular epidemiology opens that black box. It asks how changes at the molecular level (a DNA variant, an RNA transcript level, a protein concentration, a metabolite) cause, precede, accompany or result from disease. It studies the relationship in both directions: from molecule to disease, and from disease to molecule.
It is not the same discipline as biology. A molecular epidemiologist works with statistical evidence at the population level: associations, effect sizes, p-values. A molecular biologist provides the mechanistic, “definite” answers about how a change works in the cell. The two fields depend on each other. Statistical association points to candidates, and biological experiments confirm or explain the mechanism. The course frames this partnership as needing a shared vocabulary: you need to “talk biology” to read the molecular papers you build models around, and “talk bioinformatics/genetics” (variant nomenclature, databases, sequencing terms) to process the data.






ImportantCentral question of the field



Does a statistical association between a molecule and a disease reflect causality (the molecule contributes to causing the disease), or is it only correlated, a downstream consequence of disease, or a confounded association? This question runs through the whole course and is the explicit subject of Lecture 6 (Mendelian randomization).


Formal definition (the synthesis at the end of the lecture): molecular epidemiology studies how molecular variation across individuals relates to exposures, traits and disease in populations. In practice the field measures molecular variation across many individuals, links it to exposures, risk factors, disease, prognosis or treatment response, and then asks whether the associations are reproducible, predictive, mechanistically informative and potentially causal.
